raw_response:
*Speaking as this farmer, thinking out loud first — then the plan.*

---

My 4.1 mu doesn't sound like much, but it's everything I've got. I keep about 2 mu for wheat and then maize on the same land — two crops from one piece of ground. The other 2 mu I put in cotton. Cotton is harder work, especially picking, but it brings in the cash. We need both.

I don't read much. What I know about farming I learned from watching and doing. I use what my father used, adjusted for what I see working on my neighbors' fields. If the man two houses down changed something and it went well, I'll try it next year. If it went bad, I'll stay with what I do.

This season my family has three of us, but one works in town some months, so for cotton picking I'll probably need to call in a neighbor to help. That costs me something — I'll owe them labor back or pay a little.

**Wheat** goes in early October, same as everyone around here. I use the seed I saved from last harvest — buying new seed every year costs too much. I put down one bag of compound fertilizer before seeding, mixed into the soil. In spring if the wheat looks pale and thin, I'll add a little urea — maybe half a bag spread across the 2 mu. I water when I plant, once more in spring, and once when the grain is filling. Three waterings, same as most years. I hire a tractor driver to seed it — I can't afford my own machine.

**Maize** goes right after wheat comes off in early June. I have maybe five or six days at most. No time for deep plowing — I do a quick shallow pass or nothing if I'm rushed. I buy hybrid maize seed from the shop in town, not save my own. I put down some compound fertilizer when I plant and then add urea when the plants are about knee-high. Usually one watering is enough if we get some summer rain, but I'll do two if it's dry. This is the easier crop.

**Cotton** I plant in late April. It's the crop that takes the most out of me. Three fertilizer applications through the season. I irrigate twice — once when the plants are young and once when they're setting bolls. Picking is hard — I pick three or four times from September into October, same fields, looking for open bolls each time. My family does most of it but I'll probably need one hired neighbor for a few days at the peak.

My biggest worry this year is cash before wheat harvest. If I spend too much on cotton fertilizer in April–May, I might be tight. So I'll hold back a little on cotton and make sure wheat is taken care of first.
